The banyan trees outside Tai Po Mega Mall, one of which was an old banyan tree that was uprooted and fell down.

Typhoon "Hongxia" made landfall in the east, with parts of the eastern New Territories recording over 140mm of rainfall yesterday. The government said that as of 1pm on Sunday (the 26th), the government's 1823 call centre and the Fire Services Department had received a total of 331 reports of fallen trees. Tai Po was one of the hardest-hit areas for fallen trees.

Of the ten banyan trees next to Wan Lam House in Wan Tau Tong Estate, eight were blown down by strong winds. When reporters went to the scene this morning (the 27th), the remains of the eight trees had already been cleared. A Wan Tau Tong resident who has lived there for over 30 years said, "It's been many years, and we've never seen anything this severe," adding that these banyan trees had withstood typhoons for years but could not withstand the power of "Hongxia," saying, "This time they were completely uprooted."

Residents said: "This time is the worst, I couldn't believe it when I saw it." The original "banyan formation" formed by ten banyan trees was destroyed overnight, leaving only two. Residents felt it was a pity that these ten long-standing banyan trees, which had sheltered Wan Tau Tong Estate residents from wind and rain, had fallen, saying, "Let's see if we can replant them."

A large banyan tree outside Tai Po Mega Mall also could not withstand the power of Typhoon "Hongxia." The banyan trees and kapok trees here are collective memories for local residents. This time, one of the large banyan trees fell. The banyan tree, about 12 metres tall, was planted in a roughly 2-metre by 2-metre square grid, planted in a manner consistent with the "flowerpot trees" that have fallen in past storms.

A Fu Shin Estate resident said that beforehand they had heard reports that "Hongxia" was not very powerful, and only just learned that this large banyan tree outside the mall had been blown down by Typhoon "Hongxia," so "I was startled when I saw it." He shared that he "passes here every day on the way to work" and has always known the existence of this large banyan tree, expressing regret that Typhoon "Hongxia" had blown down this historic tree, saying, "What a waste of a tree." Another Tai Po resident, when asked if she hoped to save the fallen large banyan tree, said, "Of course," believing that planting large banyan trees is better than other varieties because they grow more slowly. When reporters inspected the scene in the afternoon, workers had already removed the tree.

The banyan tree fell and exposed the roots that had been buried in the soil. Leaves and dirt were scattered all over the ground, leaving a scene of devastation. Most passers-by stopped to take photos, accompanying this large banyan tree that has carried Tai Po residents' memories for many years on its "final journey."

In addition, a horsetail tree next to the cycle path along Lam Tsuen River outside the mall also fell, completely blocking the cycle path, with several bicycles abandoned in front of the fallen tree.

Apart from that, a large banyan tree next to the Kwong Fuk Estate Community Hall also could not withstand the power of "Hongxia" and fell. This morning, workers were using chainsaws on-site to clear the tree remains, and a passing child said in surprise, "What is he doing?" expressing shock at the power of Typhoon "Hongxia."

At the entrance of Cheung Chi House in Cheung Wah Estate in Fanling, two trees—a large banyan tree and a kapok tree—were blown down by the typhoon. Near a roundabout close to Cheung Chi House, the trunk of a large banyan tree was snapped by the wind, with the upper portion of the tree collapsing and obstructing traffic at the roundabout. As of morning, there were temporarily no workers on-site to remove the trees.

"Tree Doctor" Chim Chi-yung takes a pulse

Professor and consultant Chim Chi-yung of the Department of Geography and Environmental Sciences at the Education University of Hong Kong said that the reason these trees were blown down is "all the same"—it is because of insufficient planting space and soil, with roots confined, leaving the trees unable to withstand strong winds and toppling. He pointed out that the problem with these "flowerpot trees" is "extremely common." Professor Chim suggested two solutions, including digging out the original soil and re-laying it, as well as only planting short, small trees, but this would waste land resources. He said it is "a great pity" that Hong Kong has not been able to fully utilise planting resources, and described the current method of planting trees as "a waste of resources."

Suggesting the government establish a "tree rescue team"

Last September, Super Typhoon Hagens hit Hong Kong, and the government took action to save a banyan tree at Oi Man Estate in Ho Man Tin that had grown alongside residents for half a century, as well as an ancient and valuable tree, a lebbeck tree, in Kowloon Park in Tsim Sha Tsui. As for whether the trees blown down by Hongxia can be saved? Professor Chim said, "If you prop them back up, there is a way," explaining that machinery can be used to help prop the tree upright and support it to keep it alive, "they can be saved, but it's a matter of resources." He said resource allocation and whether resources are sufficient need to be considered. Professor Chim pointed out that he has repeatedly proposed establishing a "tree rescue team" to carry out training and preparation during normal times, to ensure it can be deployed in emergencies to "rescue trees," but so far there has been no sign of it being established, saying, "I believe the government has not done this."
